chapter.title: Building an Accessible Modal
chapter.description: The parts a portal does not give you for free.

blocks.text: A portal solves the layout problem. Accessibility is a separate job, and a modal that skips it is unusable with a keyboard or a screen reader.
The checklist

items: `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"` so assistive technology announces it correctly.
Focus moves into the dialog on open, and back to the trigger on close.
Focus is trapped inside while it is open - Tab must not reach the page behind.
A click on the overlay closes; a click inside does not.

blocks.text: Focus trapping is fiddly to get right. The native `<dialog>` element handles much of it, and libraries such as Radix UI or React Aria handle all of it. Write one by hand once to understand the requirements, then use a tested implementation.
Rendering into a specific container

blocks.caption: A dedicated container is easier to style and to reason about than document.body.

previous.title: What a Portal Is
previous.description: Rendering into a different DOM node while staying in the React tree.

blocks.text: `createPortal` renders children into a DOM node somewhere else in the document, while keeping them exactly where they are in the React tree.
Why you need one

A modal or tooltip nested deep inside the page inherits its ancestors' CSS. `overflow: hidden` clips it, a `transform` traps `position: fixed`, and a low `z-index` on an ancestor puts it behind other content. No amount of styling on the modal itself can escape those.

items: `overflow: hidden` on any ancestor clips the popup.
A `transform` or `filter` on an ancestor makes it the containing block for `position: fixed`.
Stacking contexts mean a child can never rise above a sibling of its ancestor.

blocks.text: Rendering into `document.body` sidesteps all three.
Events still bubble through React
This is the part that surprises people. A portal's DOM node is elsewhere, but events bubble up the **React** tree, not the DOM tree - so a click inside a portal reaches handlers on its React parent.
This catches people building click-outside handlers: a click inside a portalled dropdown still bubbles to the React parent, so a naive 'close when anything is clicked' handler closes immediately.
Context works too
Because the component stays in the React tree, it keeps access to every context and every error boundary above it. Portals change the DOM position and nothing else.

blocks.text: `StrictMode` is a development-only wrapper that surfaces unsafe patterns by doing things twice. It renders nothing itself and has no effect in production.
What it does

items: Calls component functions, initialisers, updaters and reducers **twice**, to expose impure logic.
Mounts, cleans up and remounts every component, to expose missing effect cleanup.
Warns about deprecated APIs and legacy string refs.

blocks.text: Double rendering finds impurity

The doubling is the symptom, not the disease. A component that changes external state during render is already unreliable - React may call it more than once for its own reasons, including transitions and re-entrant renders.
Double mounting finds missing cleanup
Disabling Strict Mode because effects run twice hides a real bug rather than fixing it. Any component that remounts in production - a route revisited, a list reordered - hits exactly the same path.
useInsertionEffect
A rarely used sibling of `useEffect` that runs before any DOM mutations. It exists for CSS-in-JS libraries that need to inject style rules before layout is calculated.
Unless you are writing a styling library, you will not need `useInsertionEffect`. It cannot read layout and it cannot use refs - it exists purely for the style injection timing problem.

blocks.title: Decide whether a click was inside a container
blocks.instructions: Complete isInside so it returns true when the target is the container or a descendant of it.

tests.name: A descendant counts as inside
tests.code: var b = document.createElement('div'); var c = document.createElement('span'); b.appendChild(c); return isInside(b, c) === true;

tests.name: The container itself counts
tests.code: var b = document.createElement('div'); return isInside(b, b) === true;

tests.name: An unrelated node is outside
tests.code: var b = document.createElement('div'); var o = document.createElement('p'); return isInside(b, o) === false;
